title: Classic Prayer Shawl
subtitle: Simple shell-and-chain lace in DK weight, worked as a top-down triangle
excerpt: A classic triangular shawl worked from the centre top outward in a repeating shell-and-chain pattern. DK weight yarn on a 4mm hook produces open, drapey fabric. Based on a traditional construction documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet.
sourceNotes: Construction and stitch arrangement adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet (published 1886-1897), now in the public domain. Pattern updated to modern UK crochet terminology.

glossaryTerms.definition: Five trebles worked into one stitch or space, fanning out to create a decorative scallop shape.
The gap created by skipping over one or more chains. The hook inserts into the space, not through a stitch top.

content.text: This shawl is a straightforward top-down triangle measuring approximately 165cm across the top edge and 65cm from the top to the lower point. You begin at the centre top with a small chain, then work outward in rows, adding a shell at each side on every pattern row. The stitch pattern is a repeating sequence of 5-treble shells separated by chain spaces. DK weight yarn on a 4mm hook gives an open, drapey fabric. Construction is adapted from a classic triangular shawl documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet, a late nineteenth-century needlework series now in the public domain.

Yarn: approximately 450g of DK weight yarn (a smooth wool, cotton-blend, or bamboo-blend shows the shell pattern clearly). Hook: 4mm. You will also need a tapestry needle, scissors, and a tape measure. A foam blocking mat and rust-proof pins are useful for the final shaping.

One shell repeat (5 trebles plus 2 chain spaces) measures approximately 5cm wide on a 4mm hook over the shell-and-chain pattern. Tension is not critical for a shawl: a tighter tension will produce a smaller, denser piece; a looser tension will produce a larger, more open one.
Shell: 5 tr in same ch sp

The shawl grows by two shells per right-side row: one shell is added at each edge. The centre stitch is marked and a shell always sits at the centre. Stitch counts given below refer to shells, not individual stitches, to keep the instructions readable.
Ch 6, sl st to form a ring.
Ch 4 (counts as tr + ch 1), [5 tr in ring, ch 2] twice, tr in ring, turn. (2 shells, 3 tr edge sts)
Ch 1 (does not count as st), dc in first tr, ch 2, shell in next ch-2 sp, ch 2, dc in top of centre tr, ch 2, shell in next ch-2 sp, ch 2, dc in 3rd ch of turning ch, turn. (2 shells)
Ch 4 (counts as tr + ch 1), shell in first ch-2 sp, [ch 2, shell in next ch-2 sp] to last sp, ch 1, tr in last dc, turn. (3 shells)
Ch 1 (does not count as st), dc in top of turning ch, [ch 2, shell in next ch-2 sp] across, ch 2, dc in 3rd ch of turning ch, turn. (3 shells)

Alternate Row 3 (increase RS row) with Row 4 (plain WS row), adding one extra shell on every right-side row. Continue until you have approximately 30 shells across one RS row, or until the piece measures 165cm across the top edge. The increase rows are: ch 4 at start, add a shell in the first ch sp, work shells across, ch 1, tr at end. The plain WS rows: dc at each edge, shells across. End with a WS row.
Work one round of dc evenly around the entire shawl edge. At each corner of the triangle, work 3 dc into the corner stitch to keep the fabric flat. Fasten off.

Weave in all ends securely on the wrong side. Block by soaking in cool water and pressing out excess moisture in a towel. Pin to the stated dimensions on a foam mat, easing the top edge straight and the lower point sharp. Allow to dry fully before unpinning. Blocking opens the lace pattern and defines the triangular shape.
Hand wash in cool water with a gentle detergent. Reshape and dry flat. Press gently with a damp cloth if needed. Check the yarn label for fibre-specific guidance.

This pattern establishes the core skill of working into chain spaces rather than into stitch tops. Once that feels reliable, the V-stitch triangle shawl uses a similar top-down construction with a different increase structure. For a denser triangular fabric, try a DK asymmetric wedge where increases happen on one edge only. For a finer lace result, the mohair lace shawl uses the same shell-over-chain-net principle in lace weight yarn.
